issues.legal_issue: A state legislature cannot impose a cess on entry into factory premises by treating those premises as a local area within the State’s legislative authority over local-area taxes.
material_facts: A state law authorised a cess on sugarcane entering an area specified by notification.
The notification imposed the cess on sugarcane entering areas comprising factories that crossed a specified quantity threshold.
The area relevant to the levy was factory premises, not an area administered by a municipality, panchayat, or other local body.
issues.conclusion: The state law was beyond the State Legislature’s competence and could not be saved by construing “an area” to mean a local area.
issues.legal_principle: Entry 52 of List II concerns taxes on the entry of goods into a local area, which, when within a State, means an area administered by a local body; factory premises are not such a local area. The Court followed Diamond Sugar Mills Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Jaora Sugar Mills (P) Ltd. v. State of M.P., which held that a levy on entry into factory premises did not fall within Entry 52 and that no other State or Concurrent List entry supported the law.

rule.if: challenge_to_state_taxing_law and state_levy_on_entry and levy_area_is_factory_premises and area_not_administered_by_local_body

predicates.challenge_to_state_taxing_law: The proceeding challenges the validity of a state law imposing a tax or cess.
predicates.state_levy_on_entry: The state measure imposes a levy when goods enter an area.
predicates.levy_area_is_factory_premises: The area to which the levy applies consists of factory premises.
predicates.area_not_administered_by_local_body: The area is not administered by a municipality, panchayat, or another local body.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns a state levy on entry into factory premises that are not administered by a local body, the rule treats the levy as exceeding legislative competence.

issues.legal_issue: A parliamentary law may itself impose a cess retrospectively by adopting provisions of an invalid state law, rather than validating that state law as such.
material_facts: After the state levy had been held invalid, Parliament enacted a law concerning the cess.
The parliamentary law adopted the relevant state-law provisions, notifications, orders, and rules and provided for retrospective operation.
The demand for cess concerned a period before the parliamentary law commenced.
issues.conclusion: The parliamentary law did not validate the invalid state law; it made a parliamentary law concerning the cess and gave that law retrospective operation.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Sugarcane Cess (Validation) Act, 1961, the relevant state-law provisions and instruments were adopted as part of the parliamentary enactment, which operated retrospectively. The Court relied on Jaora Sugar Mills (P) Ltd. v. State of M.P. for the principle that the resulting command to pay was Parliament’s own law, not a validation of the invalid state statutes.

predicates.challenge_to_retrospective_cess_law: The proceeding challenges a parliamentary measure that applies retrospectively to a cess.
predicates.parliament_enacted_cess_measure: Parliament enacted a law concerning the cess.
predicates.parliamentary_law_adopted_prior_levy_pro: The parliamentary law incorporated the relevant provisions and instruments previously used to impose or collect the cess.
predicates.parliamentary_law_operates_retrospective: The parliamentary law provides that its operation extends to an earlier period.

issues.definition: When Parliament enacts a retrospective cess measure adopting the earlier levy provisions, the rule treats the obligation as arising under the parliamentary law.

issues.legal_issue: A prior court order quashing a cess notification does not prevent recovery when a later parliamentary law expressly gives retrospective effect to the cess notwithstanding court orders.
material_facts: A court had quashed the notification imposing the cess.
A later parliamentary enactment stated that the cess would be deemed validly imposed, assessed, or collected notwithstanding any judgment, decree, or order of a court.
The subsequent recovery demand related to the cess covered by that enactment.
issues.conclusion: The prior order quashing the notification did not prevent recovery of the cess after the parliamentary enactment took effect.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Sugarcane Cess (Validation) Act, 1961, expressly applied notwithstanding judgments, decrees, or orders and deemed covered cess validly imposed, assessed, or collected. The Court held that the earlier mandamus could not avail the appellant after that enactment.

rule.if: cess_recovery_challenge and prior_court_order_quashed_levy and later_parliamentary_law_applies_notwithstanding_court_orders and later_law_covers_the_cess

predicates.cess_recovery_challenge: The proceeding challenges recovery of a cess.
predicates.prior_court_order_quashed_levy: A court had previously set aside the measure imposing the cess.
predicates.later_parliamentary_law_applies_notwiths: A later parliamentary law expressly applies despite prior court orders.
predicates.later_law_covers_the_cess: The later law covers the cess for which recovery is sought.

issues.definition: When a later parliamentary law covers the cess and expressly applies despite the earlier order setting aside its levy, the rule treats that order as no bar to recovery.

issues.legal_issue: A collector need not make a separate formal assessment order before recovering a cess where the governing scheme requires the collector to check the occupier’s returns and deposits and recover any shortfall.
material_facts: The governing law and rules required the factory occupier to keep daily records, submit monthly returns, and deposit the cess due after the crushing season.
The rules empowered the collector to check the occupier’s deposits against the returns and to give written notice requiring payment of any shortfall.
The occupier disputed the demand but acknowledged a lower amount as payable.

The collector considered the matter and directed recovery of the cess due; a subordinate official demanded more than the amount acknowledged, and the High Court limited recovery to the acknowledged amount.
issues.conclusion: The law and rules did not require a separate formal assessment order before collection. The recovery was properly confined to the amount acknowledged as due.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1958, and rules 60–63 of the 1959 Rules assigned the collector the task of checking deposits against returns and notifying the occupier of a shortfall. “Assess” is comprehensive and may include computation, determination of tax payable, and collection or recovery; a formal order is not invariably required, particularly where the assessee’s identity is not disputed. The Court held that the collector’s responsibility under the rules was to ensure that the full cess due was credited to the treasury.

rule.if: challenge_to_cess_recovery and occupier_required_to_report_and_deposit_cess and collector_required_to_check_returns_and_deposits and collector_found_or_checked_a_shortfall and assessee_identity_not_disputed

predicates.challenge_to_cess_recovery: The proceeding challenges the recovery of a cess from an occupier.
predicates.occupier_required_to_report_and_deposit_: The occupier was required to report the relevant quantities and deposit the cess due.
predicates.collector_required_to_check_returns_and_: The collector was responsible for checking the occupier’s returns and deposits against the amount due.
predicates.collector_found_or_checked_a_shortfall: The collector checked the amount deposited and determined that a shortfall remained, or directed recovery of the amount due.
predicates.assessee_identity_not_disputed: There was no dispute about the identity of the person liable for the cess.

issues.definition: When the occupier must report and deposit the cess, the collector must check for a shortfall, and the liable person’s identity is undisputed, the rule permits recovery without a separate formal assessment while limiting recovery to the amount found due.
